flashcards.back_definition: Manipulating people, not machines, into an action that helps an attacker: clicking a link, revealing a password, wiring money or holding a door open.
flashcards.back_example: A caller posing as the IT helpdesk talks an employee into reading out a one-time code.
flashcards.back_confusion: A software exploit targets a flaw in code; social engineering targets predictable flaws in human decision-making.
flashcards.back_hook: Hack the human, not the computer.

flashcards.front: Name the four pressure tactics that appear again and again in social engineering messages.
flashcards.back_definition: Urgency (act now), authority (I am your boss, IT, the tax office), scarcity (only 3 left) and intimidation (or you will be fined, fired or arrested).
flashcards.back_example: "This is the IRS. Pay within 24 hours or face arrest" stacks authority, urgency and intimidation.
flashcards.back_confusion: Tactics are not exclusive: one message often stacks several, and stacking multiplies the pressure.

flashcards.front: Urgency vs scarcity: what is the difference?
flashcards.back_definition: Urgency is manufactured time pressure ("your account closes in 1 hour"). Scarcity is implied limited supply ("only 3 spots left", "exclusive offer").
flashcards.back_example: "Verify now or lose access tonight" is urgency; "Last 2 free gift cards" is scarcity.
flashcards.back_confusion: Both rush you, but urgency is about time running out and scarcity is about the thing running out.
flashcards.back_hook: Urgency watches the clock; scarcity watches the shelf.

flashcards.front: What should you do the moment a message makes you feel rushed or afraid?
flashcards.back_definition: Treat the emotional pressure itself as the red flag: slow down and verify the request through a separate, trusted channel you look up yourself.
flashcards.back_example: Call the bank on the number printed on your card, not the number in the email.
flashcards.back_confusion: Replying to the message, or calling a number it gives you, is not verification: the attacker controls that channel.
flashcards.back_hook: Pulse up? Pause and phone out.

flashcards.back_definition: Covertly extracting sensitive information through ordinary-seeming conversation, so the target never realises they are giving it away.
flashcards.back_example: "I heard your VPN uses port 1433, or was it 443?" invites the target to correct a deliberately wrong statement.
flashcards.back_confusion: Pretexting is the invented story (I'm from IT); elicitation is the conversational technique used to pull details out.
flashcards.back_hook: People love to correct you, and that is the trap.

flashcards.back_definition: Inventing a believable scenario and role, the pretext, so a request for access or information seems normal.
flashcards.back_example: A caller says they are from the helpdesk, names your manager, then asks you to reset a password.
flashcards.back_confusion: Tailgating is physical (following someone through a door); pretexting is a story told over phone, email or in person.
flashcards.back_hook: A pretext is a pre-written script.

flashcards.front: How do typosquatting and a homograph attack differ?
flashcards.back_definition: Typosquatting registers a lookalike domain using typos or swapped characters (paypa1.com, g00gle.com). A homograph attack uses visually identical characters from another script, such as a Cyrillic "а" in place of a Latin "a".
flashcards.back_example: paypa1.com (digit 1 for letter l) is typosquatting; аpple.com with a Cyrillic first letter is a homograph.
flashcards.back_confusion: Both are lookalike domains; only the homograph uses characters from a different alphabet, so it can look pixel-identical.
flashcards.back_hook: Typo = wrong key; homograph = wrong alphabet.

flashcards.front: Name four technical signs that a link is malicious.
flashcards.back_definition: A lookalike domain, a raw IP address instead of a hostname, visible link text that differs from the real href, and a link that ends in an executable file.
flashcards.back_example: Text says https://mybank.com but the href is http://192.0.2.7/login.exe.
flashcards.back_confusion: A padlock (HTTPS) is not one of the safe signs: attackers get free TLS certificates for malicious domains.
flashcards.back_hook: Read URLs right to left: the real domain sits just before the first single slash.

flashcards.front: What is a double extension, and why does it work?
flashcards.back_definition: A filename such as report.pdf.exe that disguises an executable as a harmless document. Windows hides known extensions by default, so the user sees only report.pdf.
flashcards.back_example: invoice.pdf.exe opens as a program, not a PDF.
flashcards.back_confusion: The last extension decides what the file is; everything before it is just part of the name.
flashcards.back_hook: Only the last extension tells the truth.

flashcards.front: Phishing, spear phishing, whaling and smishing: what is each?
flashcards.back_definition: Phishing is mass impersonation to steal credentials or deliver malware. Spear phishing targets a specific person using researched details. Whaling is spear phishing aimed at executives. Smishing is phishing by SMS.
flashcards.back_example: A text "UPS: your package is held, reschedule at bit.ly/..." is smishing.
flashcards.back_confusion: Vishing is voice phishing (phone calls), which AI voice cloning makes more convincing.
flashcards.back_hook: Fish in a net, a spear for one fish, a harpoon for the whale.

flashcards.back_definition: An attacker impersonates or takes over an executive's or supplier's email to authorise fraudulent payments or obtain sensitive data.
flashcards.back_example: In 2019 a European subsidiary of Toyota Boshoku was tricked into wiring about $37 million to an attacker's account.
flashcards.back_confusion: BEC often carries no malware or link at all: just a convincing request, so filters that look for payloads miss it.
flashcards.back_hook: No virus needed, just a believable boss.

flashcards.front: What do SPF, DKIM and DMARC each check?
flashcards.back_definition: SPF (RFC 7208) lists which servers may send mail for a domain. DKIM (RFC 6376) adds a cryptographic signature to the message. DMARC (RFC 7489) tells receivers what to do when SPF or DKIM fail and aligns them with the visible From domain.
flashcards.back_example: v=DMARC1; p=reject; rua=mailto:dmarc@example.com tells receivers to reject mail that fails.
flashcards.back_confusion: None of them stops a lookalike domain: an attacker who owns paypa1.com can pass SPF, DKIM and DMARC for paypa1.com.
flashcards.back_hook: SPF = who may send, DKIM = signed seal, DMARC = the rulebook.

flashcards.front: Why is WebAuthn / FIDO2 called phishing-resistant?
flashcards.back_definition: The browser binds the login to the exact domain (the origin). A security key or passkey will not produce a valid response for a fake site, so there is nothing for the attacker to relay.
flashcards.back_example: A user on micros0ft-login.net taps their key, and the login simply fails.
flashcards.back_confusion: TOTP codes and push approvals can be phished in real time; origin-bound authenticators cannot be.
flashcards.back_hook: The key checks the address so the human doesn't have to.

flashcards.front: What consequences can a victim face after a successful social engineering attack?
flashcards.back_definition: Account takeover, stolen money, malware or ransomware on the device, leaked personal or company data, and attackers moving on to the victim's contacts.
flashcards.back_example: In July 2020 attackers phoned Twitter staff, got into internal admin tools and hijacked high-profile accounts for a cryptocurrency scam.
flashcards.back_confusion: The damage rarely stops at one person: a stolen login reaches every system and person that account can reach.
